html:
A small mosque by Mimar Sinan in the market streets near the Spice Bazaar in Istanbul, built for the grand vizier Rüstem Pasha, the husband of Suleiman's daughter Mihrimah. Rüstem died in 1561 and Suleiman approved the project the next year. There is no foundation inscription; the records suggest it was built from 1561 to 1563.

It stands on a high terrace over vaulted shops whose rents paid for its upkeep, reached by narrow stairs at the corners. The hall is an octagon set in a rectangle, its dome resting on four half domes placed on the diagonals. The mosque is known for its Iznik tiles, which cover almost every wall inside and the front of the porch: about 2,300 tiles in some 80 floral and geometric patterns. They include early use of the tomato-red glaze called Armenian bole, which became a mark of Iznik ware.

Sinan usually let the structure speak and kept decoration sparse; no other mosque uses Iznik tiles so lavishly, and in later mosques he used them more sparingly. Rüstem Pasha himself lies in a tiled tomb by Sinan in the garden of the Şehzade Mosque. The mosque reopened for worship in 2021 after a long restoration.
